Source links: fixed ports and environment wiring, live-host builds, unbounded history query, statement import, SMS batch boundary, JSON parsing, IMAP poller, OTP lifetime/hash, SMTP sender.

Database connections: scale the budget, not connections per user

The compose default is 10 connections per API instance and 10 per auth instance. Two app hosts can therefore open up to 40 application connections before workers, migrations, monitoring and provider services. More replicas multiply the potential total. Audit all pools and their maximum replica counts together, as recommended by node-postgres pool-sizing guidance.

For direct/session connections, budget:
  API replicas × API pool max
+ auth replicas × auth pool max
+ worker pools + platform/maintenance/admin reserve
<= the actual PostgreSQL connection budget

With a transaction pooler, separately budget client connections
and the actual backend connections opened by every pooler/direct client.

Worked example only: if a PostgreSQL instance allowed 60 total connections, reserving 20 for platform/maintenance/administration and using two API pools of 5, two auth pools of 5 and one worker pool of 5 totals 45 including the reserve, leaving 15 headroom. This is not the verified limit of the current server and not a proposed universal setting. Measure pool wait time and throughput; increasing max connections can worsen memory pressure and contention.

If using Supabase, distinguish pooler client limits from PostgreSQL backend limits, and count platform connections in the same instance budget (official pooling and limits). Transaction pooling needs compatibility verification: the product's transaction-local RLS context is a useful starting point, but session advisory locks such as B02 cannot simply be moved unchanged. Keep migrations, restores and session-dependent operations on appropriate direct/session connections. Verify support for the separate auth database and intended roles rather than just changing a port number.

OTP delivery may be the first launch bottleneck

The environment template names Gmail SMTP; that is not proof of the live email provider. If a consumer Gmail account is still being used, it is not suitable for a 20,000-signup campaign: Google's documentation describes a sending limit around 500 messages/day and temporary sending blocks (Gmail limits). More API RAM does not change that quota.

For a modeled 20,000 email signups in ten minutes, even one code per user requires roughly 33 accepted sends/second. A planning allowance of two attempts per user raises that to approximately 67/second and 40,000 sends/day. Confirm an approved transactional-email quota above the chosen scenario—for example, at least 75 sends/second and 50,000/day for this assumed case—plus sender-domain verification, SPF/DKIM/DMARC, bounce/complaint handling and delivery monitoring. These are proposed requirements, not a provider capacity purchase or guarantee of inbox placement.

Keep OTP delivery ahead of noncritical notifications. If moving it to a queue, enforce expiry-aware processing and bounded retries: a code arriving after its 120-second lifetime is not a successful sign-in experience. The current response reports SMTP acceptance, not final inbox delivery. An asynchronous design must introduce an honest pending/delivery-failure contract rather than immediately claiming that every queued code was sent. Never expose OTPs in monitoring, caches or ordinary logs.

Storage planning: ledger, files, logs and backups are separate

For illustration, assume 3–6 KiB per imported transaction including its typical observation/index share. This is an unvalidated planning range, not extrapolation from a representative production dataset. Other account data, WAL, temporary files, bloat, replicas, backups and receipt images are excluded. Replace it with measured bytes per successful import on a production-shaped staging dataset.

20,000 users importingPotential canonical transactionsIllustrative ledger/observation/index allocation
100 distinct transactions each2 million5.72–11.44 GiB
500 distinct transactions each10 million28.61–57.22 GiB
1,000 distinct transactions each20 million57.22–114.44 GiB

Provision room for WAL generated during bursts, autovacuum, index maintenance and temporary query files. Start with an operational goal of at least 25–30% free space plus separately sized maintenance/restore scratch requirements; a full clone or index rebuild can exceed that reserve. Monitor growth rate and time-to-full, not only a percentage. Choose adequate SSD IOPS/throughput as well as capacity; leave autovacuum healthy and avoid long transactions that prevent cleanup.

If the production database follows the Supabase template, check the actual plan before launch. Current documentation says a Free project can become read-only above a 500 MB database quota, independently of the advertised disk allocation. Paid disk expansion also has conditions and cooldowns; do not rely on last-minute automatic growth during a major import (database versus disk quotas). This is conditional provider guidance, not a claim that PandaPay is currently on that plan.

Storage classRecommendation specific to this application
Financial/auth rowsKeep authoritative structured records in PostgreSQL, with tested retention for OTPs, sessions, raw imports, sync/change logs and operational history. Do not delete financial history merely to recover space. Review section 10's small retirement candidates for simplicity, not meaningful capacity savings.
Receipt filesThey are local-only today. If cloud receipts are added, use private object storage with authenticated signed access, bounded/compressed uploads, per-user quotas, lifecycle/erasure and DB metadata references—not base64 images in transaction rows or a single app VM's disk. As an example, 20,000 users × 10 receipts × 500 KiB is about 95.4 GiB of new objects, separate from the ledger.
App disk and logsCompose rotates container logs at 10 MB × 5 files per service. OS/nginx logs, image layers/build caches and predeployment dumps are separate; cap and monitor them too. Prebuilt images reduce live-host build space/CPU pressure.
BackupsThe scheduled backup currently targets the product DB and local Docker volume with 30-day retention. Extend verified recovery to auth as well, encrypt copies off-host and set a tested recovery-point/recovery-time objective. PITR is recommended where supported for an acceptable recovery window; logical dumps remain useful.
Backup/restore overheadThe deploy script's predeploy dumps use a separate directory and are not covered by the nightly pandapay-*.dump cleanup pattern. Add an explicit successful-backup retention policy. The restore drill currently creates its temporary database on the source PostgreSQL instance; move substantial drills to an isolated restore environment so a full extra copy does not exhaust production disk/CPU.

Budget backup storage from measured compressed dump size × retained copies, plus auth, WAL/PITR and any replicated/off-site copies. For example, if the combined daily logical dumps later measured 20 GiB, 30 full copies would consume roughly 600 GiB before other copies—not 20 GiB. Do not assume a compression ratio or that a local Docker volume survives VM loss. Object-file recovery is separate: Supabase database backups, for example, do not include Storage API objects (backup scope).

Evidence: scheduled dump and retention, predeployment dump path, restore drill. A dump that can be listed is an initial integrity check; only an actual restore and application verification establishes useful recovery evidence.

Backpressure and graceful degradation on small servers

  1. Put bounded admission at the edge and within services: global capacity, correctly trusted IP limits, account/challenge limits and maximum in-flight expensive operations. Use controlled 429/503 responses and retry guidance; the mobile app needs bounded exponential backoff with jitter rather than a retry storm.
  2. Prioritize authentication, small financial writes and interactive reads. Queue resumable imports, mailbox catch-up and noncritical delivery with separate concurrency budgets and per-account fairness. Return a job ID only after the job is durably recorded; acknowledge completed financial work only after the relevant commit.
  3. Preserve the existing offline experience. Show clearly dated cached information when appropriate, retain pending edits safely and surface an honest processing state. Never display stale cached balances as newly confirmed server results or bypass authorization during an outage.
  4. Keep caches, queue length/age, request bodies, response pages and pool waits bounded. Establish what happens when any bound is reached. A longer in-memory queue on a 1–2 GiB server can turn a transient burst into an out-of-memory restart.
  5. Define Redis/provider failure policies explicitly. Abuse-control outages must not create unlimited OTP access; failed background work must remain recoverable without duplicating ledger effects. A dead-letter/review path and safe replay are needed for terminal failures.

What to monitor and when to add capacity

These are initial alert/scale thresholds to calibrate in testing, not values measured on the current servers. Start with actionable user-impact metrics and avoid autoscaling solely from one instantaneous CPU reading.

SignalInitial trigger or targetResponse
App CPU and latencySustained CPU around 65–70% for 10 minutes, or rising p95 latency/pool wait at the accepted load. Track auth hashing and event-loop delay separately.Investigate the bottleneck; add/prewarm app capacity if CPU-bound, or fix DB/provider waits if those dominate.
RAMAvailable host memory below roughly 20–25%, sustained container RSS near its tested cap, abnormal GC, or any OOM kill.Reduce admitted concurrency/expensive work and increase RAM or replicas as appropriate. Account for native buffers/TLS, not only the JavaScript heap. Reserve capacity for a deploy/backup peak.
PostgreSQLRising pool acquisition time, active connection pressure, slow query fingerprints, lock waits, CPU/IO saturation or overdue vacuum.Shorten transactions, tune justified queries/indexes and throttle workers first; resize DB when capacity is genuinely exhausted. Never blindly multiply all pools.
OTPProvider rejection/throttling, acceptance latency and real delivery time. Proposed delivery objective: p95 below 30 seconds, safely inside the current 120-second validity.Confirm quota/reputation and bound delivery concurrency. Expiry-aware retries and explicit failures; do not keep sending unusable old codes.
Background workOldest job age, processing time, retries and per-account fairness—not queue length alone.Add workers only within the shared DB/provider budget; separate slow providers and pause noncritical jobs during foreground overload.
Disk and recoveryStart warnings near 70% and critical alerts near 80–85%, or sooner if forecast exhaustion precedes the next resize window. Track backup age/restore results and WAL growth.Expand ahead of campaigns; resolve runaway WAL/retention/log growth. Restore readiness must be checked independently of available disk.

Define a tested maximum replica count so autoscaling cannot exhaust database connections or provider quota. Keep an explicit cost budget/alert for compute, database storage/IO, backups, object storage/egress and email volume. Pre-provision for announced campaigns; autoscaling may react after the initial spike has already arrived.

How to prove the launch capacity safely

  1. Build a staging environment with the intended production topology, RLS roles, connection limits and production-shaped histories/indexes. Use synthetic accounts and realistic data distributions, including large histories. Keep the load generator on a separate machine.
  2. Measure actual requests per onboarding session, query counts, payload sizes, import write amplification and bytes per imported record. Test sign-in, OTP verification, home summaries, recommendations, paged history, sync and concurrent imports—not only /health.
  3. Model arrival rates as well as active users. An open arrival model can maintain offered load when responses slow; a closed virtual-user loop can otherwise hide overload by sending less work (k6 workload-model guidance). Calibrate scenario rates from observed flows rather than treating a virtual user as one request/second.
  4. Ramp through calibrated scenarios such as 20, 50, 100, 250 and 500 total RPS as appropriate; stop safely on saturation. Include a ten-minute spike, an hour of steady load and a longer soak, with bounded import backlog. These rates are test scenarios, not already supported capacity claims.
  5. Use a staging email sink and full secure test-account verification to exercise hashing/DB work without sending thousands of real emails. Run a small, separately approved delivery canary against the real provider to validate quota/acceptance/delivery; a sink cannot prove deliverability. Never enable a test OTP bypass on an internet-accessible production service.
  6. Exercise one app VM unavailable, process restarts, Redis failure, slow/unavailable SMTP, DB pressure and worker replay. Assert no cross-account reads, missing committed writes, duplicate financial effects, unbounded retries or lost durable jobs. Recheck RLS isolation across reused pooled connections.
  7. Record maximum admitted throughput at the chosen reliability targets, resource peaks, pool waits and backlog drain time. Draft targets for discussion: light interactive reads p95 under 1 second and fewer than 1% unexpected 5xx responses at admitted load, no OOM, and jobs recovering within a declared completion window. Report intentional admission rejections separately so a low 5xx rate cannot conceal rejected users. Confirm the degraded/failover target as well as the healthy target.

No load test was run as part of this report update. Production load generation, provider-scale sends and infrastructure spending require a separate approved execution plan.

Recommended order before marketing

  1. Correctness/security first: resolve the existing identity/authorization findings, worker-role/lock issues and migration/recovery gaps. Do not amplify known vulnerabilities to a larger audience.
  2. Protect the small server: remove live-host builds, measure/cap memory and concurrency, align payload limits, bound history reads correctly and throttle imports. Confirm quota-approved OTP delivery and two-database off-host recovery.
  3. Add the campaign topology: health-checked load balancing, two app VMs, shared abuse controls and an explicit durable worker deployment. Set the aggregate connection budget and a maximum replica count before adding replicas.
  4. Prove and reserve capacity: production-shaped load/failure tests, operational alerts, cost limits, restore evidence and prewarmed resources. Publish a measured launch envelope and a controlled overload/runbook plan.
  5. Scale further only where measured: database CPU/RAM/IO upgrades, more bounded workers/app replicas, selective caching and possibly stale-tolerant read replicas. Partitioning, sharding and more independently deployed services need demonstrated volume/operational benefit; they are not prerequisites simply because 20,000 people may register.

Bottom line: plan for burst arrivals and imported histories, not a registered-user count. The recommended baseline is two modest app servers, an independently sized PostgreSQL instance, bounded background workers, shared limits and a real OTP delivery budget. The exact safe throughput must be established by testing; none is certified by the current small local database or by this report.

14. CDN, Redis and the supporting services PandaPay needs

23 October status: CDN/WAF/result-cache choices, freshness/invalidation and deployment topology remain proposals. Hosted OTP/enumeration/replacement controls now use PostgreSQL atomic buckets and fail closed on storage failure; Redis is not required for those controls. Legacy general/admin/user limiter and Redis recovery behavior remain separate work. No CDN rollout, cache-hit/load result or private-cache isolation certification is claimed.

Recommendation: use a CDN selectively for public content; use Redis first for shared abuse controls, then for measured read hotspots; keep PostgreSQL authoritative; and use durable workers for slow work. These are different layers, not interchangeable solutions. A CDN will not fix an expensive uncached financial query, Redis will not increase an email provider's quota, and neither replaces the authentication repairs in this report.

This section maps established scaling patterns to current PandaPay source and official infrastructure documentation. It is not a claim that every large application uses one particular stack. No live CDN/Redis deployment was inspected or changed, and no provider purchase or application implementation was performed.

Which layer handles which problem?

LayerJobRecommended PandaPay use
CDN / edge cacheReuse identical public responses near users, reducing origin bandwidth and repeated requests.Public catalogue/categories under explicit cache rules; public remote logos/assets and legal pages. Never a blanket cache-everything rule on API/auth hosts.
WAF / edge abuse controlsReject some unwanted traffic before it consumes app resources. This is distinct from response caching.Protect API/auth hosts with API-compatible limits and origin protection, while leaving private responses uncached. Still enforce account/challenge policy in the backend.
Load balancerRoute requests to healthy app replicas.The two-app-server campaign topology from section 13, with readiness and connection draining. A CDN account is not automatically a configured multi-origin load balancer.
RedisFast shared expiring state or reusable server-side results.Coordinate OTP/account/IP limits across replicas. Consider versioned catalogue/summary caches only after measuring; keep security state separate from evictable caches.
PostgreSQL + bounded poolsAuthoritative financial/auth data, constraints and transactional changes.Preserve the current two logical databases and RLS boundaries; optimize actual queries and enforce the total connection budget.
Durable queue/outbox + workersKeep slow/retryable work out of interactive requests without losing it on a crash.Large imports, IMAP catch-up, notification delivery and cleanup. Persist jobs/events and make processing idempotent.
Object storageDurable files without tying them to one VM.Off-host encrypted backups; future private cloud receipts. A CDN is a delivery layer, not the durable origin or backup.
Device cache + observabilityAvoid unnecessary network calls and establish whether the system works under load.Preserve account-scoped SQLite/offline behavior; measure request volume, cache hits, invalidation, pool wait, queue age and user-visible latency.

Exactly what should use a CDN?

Content / routeCDN decisionPandaPay-specific guardrail
GET /catalogueYes, a strong initial candidate. Current handler reads the same public export view for callers without user context.Cache only the intentionally published device projection. Publication, corrections and withdrawal need bounded freshness and invalidation. Never substitute /admin/cards or a raw table dump. Resolve existing publication/security issues independently.
GET /categoriesYes. Standard categories are public.Keep this distinct from authenticated /user-categories. Include any future response-shaping locale/schema inputs in the key.
Public bank/issuer logos and other remotely loaded shared artworkYes, when PandaPay controls the licensed asset origin. Home currently loads an issuer logo URL over the network.Use optimized, versioned image paths and a managed asset domain. Do not proxy arbitrary user-provided URLs or copy third-party images without permission. Existing third-party CDN URLs may already be efficient.
Card faces, bundled icons and installed Flutter assetsNo additional CDN just for these. CardVisual currently draws the card face locally.A CDN cannot speed up a CustomPaint operation or an asset already installed on the device. Avoid adding a remote dependency where none is needed.
Public legal/help pages and a future public web front end's static filesYes. nginx already serves /legal/ independently of the API container.Use modest freshness for mutable legal HTML; hashed public web assets can use long freshness. Authenticated admin HTML/data, test tools and this sensitive audit report are not public-site assets.
Profiles, wallets, user cards, transaction histories, balances, reward summaries and personalized recommendationsNo shared CDN response cache in the proposed design.Keep current authentication/authorization on origin requests. A profile ID in a query string or Vary: Authorization is not sufficient justification to publicly cache financial responses.
OTP, login, verification, refresh, logout, recovery, admin APIs and incoming webhooksBypass response caching.They can traverse an edge security proxy, but must retain correct method/body/auth semantics. Never cache tokens, OTPs, sensitive errors or Set-Cookie responses.
Future receipt photos, bank statements and account exportsPrivate object storage first; private CDN only if later justified. Receipts are local-only today.Authenticate ownership before issuing short-lived access. A private CDN must validate access even on a cache hit and prevent direct-origin bypass. Do not publish the bucket to improve cache hit rate.
Database dumps, operational exports, logs and audit artifactsNever public CDN content.Private backup storage, restricted operator access and a retention/recovery policy instead.

Source evidence: public catalogue handler, public versus user categories, network-loaded issuer logo, locally drawn card visual, legal-page origin, existing client catalogue cache. The HTTP catalogue repository fetches the full JSON response; surrounding providers already supply caching/fallback behavior, so its older no-offline comment is not an accurate description of the whole current app.

Safe cache policy and freshness contract

Start with default bypass on API/auth, then explicitly allow only selected public GET/HEAD responses on exact routes. Require an eligible successful response, the expected content type, no credentials/cookies and no user-specific body. Preserve bypass for other methods, private paths and errors. Use path normalization and test encoded/suffix routes so an apparent .css extension cannot turn a private API response into a static asset.

The following are illustrative starting policies to validate, not deployed headers or measured optimal TTLs:

Response classProposed policyFreshness/invalidation contract
Sensitive API/auth responsesCache-Control: private, no-store plus an explicit CDN bypass rule.An edge rule must not override the bypass. The app's deliberate account-scoped offline storage is a separate lifecycle, not permission for an HTTP intermediary to retain these responses.
Mutable public catalogue/categoriesExample: Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, s-maxage=300, with a stable content validator.A five-minute edge window is acceptable only if product policy permits it. Publishing/corrections/withdrawal should trigger purge or a version transition with retries and alerting. Do not promise instant withdrawal merely because a purge was requested.
Content-hashed public images/JS/CSSExample: Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable.Only for URLs whose bytes never change. A different file gets a different URL. Keep mutable HTML/version manifests short-lived or revalidated.

Cache eligibility and TTL behavior are provider-specific; these proposed policies must be tested on the chosen service. Cloudflare, for example, does not cache JSON/HTML by default, so merely enabling its proxy does not establish catalogue caching (default cache behavior). Its cache rules can override origin instructions, and no-cache means revalidation rather than no storage (cache-control reference).

Use one explicit global catalogue publication revision that covers edits, dependent rule/category changes, deletions and withdrawals; do not assume the largest per-card version covers all changes. Include every legitimate response variant in the cache key, while rejecting/normalizing irrelevant query parameters to avoid unlimited variants. Never let untrusted forwarding headers choose another cache namespace or origin.

ETags/304 responses reduce transferred bytes but do not automatically eliminate the database query needed to build the body. A precomputed publication snapshot/version can avoid repeated serialization/queries. The current HTTP repository expects status 200; introducing conditional requests needs supported 304 handling and a retained cached body, not just a new header. Update client compatibility and version invalidation together.

For future private-file delivery, a normal object-store signed URL placed behind a generic public cache is not sufficient: the object store might never see a cache hit. Use a private-distribution access mechanism that verifies the request at the edge and restricts the origin. AWS documents this separation in its signed-URL flow and private-origin controls. Signed links are bearer access while valid; redact them from logs and acknowledge that expiry does not erase a file already downloaded.

Where Redis helps this application

PriorityRedis useDesign and failure behavior
First, before multiple auth replicasShared OTP/account/IP abuse counters and existing active-challenge tracking.Use atomic expiring operations, purpose/challenge binding and the authoritative database's verification rules. Define restart/outage behavior so a replica or Redis restart cannot silently reset all security guarantees. Never store raw OTPs/tokens as an ordinary cache optimization.
Next, only if still useful after CDN/client cachingPublic published catalogue/category origin cache.Shared versioned cache-aside: check Redis, load the allowed DB projection on a miss, then populate a bounded entry. A cache miss is not a release of authorization controls. Avoid maintaining another large stale copy if CDN/client hit rates already remove most work.
After measuring summary-query costAccount-scoped dashboard/spending aggregates.Key by account, period, relevant filters and a data/calculation revision. Invalidate after successful financial mutations/import/reconciliation. A revisioned key helps prevent an old concurrent loader from repopulating the new generation; recheck versions/consistency when needed. No shared CDN cache for these results.
Later, if provider requests across replicas are a measured hotspotSelected public nearby-discovery provider results.The existing discovery module already has local maps, in-flight dedupe and a rounded-location key. Preserve provider terms, bounds and location minimization if moving reusable results into Redis. Do not turn precise user-location histories or personalized results into a shared public cache.
Not as a disposable cacheCanonical transactions, reward ledger, durable import job payloads or the only record of a session revocation.Keep authoritative state and required financial idempotency in PostgreSQL. A queue product built on Redis needs an explicitly engineered persistence/recovery configuration, not the settings used for an evictable response cache.

Cache-aside is a standard pattern, but it needs invalidation and protection when many callers miss together. Use bounded single-flight loading, short owner-token leases where appropriate, TTL jitter and bounded waiting; do not release someone else's lease or let every timeout launch an unlimited fallback query. Redis describes these mechanics in its Node cache-aside example. These mechanisms protect cache population; they are not substitutes for database transactions or durable financial deduplication.

Redis details to fix or verify in the existing source

  1. Wire it into the deployed topology. Auth supports REDIS_URL, but production compose does not pass it and defines no Redis service. That is a deployment-source gap, not proof of Redis absence in production. Add private connectivity/TLS and scoped credentials through the deployment secret mechanism; never expose Redis to mobile clients or the public internet.
  2. Make counter-plus-expiry atomic where Redis remains. The original Redis helpers used INCR and EXPIRE separately; hosted OTP counters now use transactional PostgreSQL storage with fixed expiry. Remaining legacy Redis paths still need review. Interruption between them can leave a counter without its intended TTL. Use a tested atomic script/function or equivalent algorithm and verify partial-failure/concurrency behavior. This exact failure pattern is discussed in the Redis counter/rate-limiter reference.
  3. Recover from connectivity failures deliberately. The Redis client latches redisInitFailed and can return null without retrying; the host/port path also disables automatic reconnection. Define bounded reconnect/backoff and readiness/alerts, and test Redis recovery without restarting every app instance. Reconcile fallback policy across both services.
  4. Separate security counters from disposable data. Use independently budgeted instances or provider databases with genuinely independent resource/eviction settings—not just different prefixes or Redis SELECT database numbers on the same instance. An allkeys eviction policy can remove security limits; noeviction can instead reject new writes, which also needs a conservative failure policy. Size for abuse-driven key growth and expire identities/challenges appropriately.
  5. Bound memory and cold-start load. Set maxmemory below available RAM, allow room for overhead/persistence buffers, monitor evictions/OOM/latency and choose policy by purpose. Redis documents these tradeoffs in its eviction guidance. Optional cache failure should cause bounded degradation, not a flood of replacement DB queries; security-store failure must not become unlimited admission.

Evidence: legacy Redis connection/retry behavior, implemented PostgreSQL OTP store, remaining user-route counter and fallback, compose environment, existing discovery cache. Redis/cache proposals are not newly reproduced production incidents or completed deployments; the PostgreSQL security-store implementation is separately recorded in the status ledger.

Other scalable-application building blocks: add selectively

NeedRecommendation nowWhat not to add without evidence
Durable import/IMAP/delivery workStart with a PostgreSQL-backed job/outbox mechanism or one managed queue, with ownership leases, retries, dead-letter review and idempotent replay. The outbox addresses the commit-versus-send gap in SD01.Kafka, multiple brokers and a Redis queue are not all required together. Do not rely on Pub/Sub or an in-memory array for work that must survive a crash.
Database efficiencyCorrect pagination/aggregates, justified indexes, short transactions and bounded pools; consider a compatible server-side pooler.No automatic read-replica routing or write scalability just because a pooler/CDN exists. Sharding and a database-per-feature are premature without measured need.
File handlingPrivate object storage and bounded uploads if cloud files are introduced; public asset delivery can use the CDN.Do not route large files through the low-RAM API unnecessarily or store images/base64 in Redis. Keep private attachments separate from public logo buckets.
Provider resilienceIndependent concurrency/timeout/retry budgets for SMTP, push, discovery and IMAP; quota monitoring and circuit-break/degraded behavior.A CDN is not an SMTP relay and cannot solve delayed OTP email. Keep provider failure from exhausting every DB connection.
Visibility and operationsCentral privacy-preserving logs, latency/error/saturation metrics, alerts, restore evidence, immutable releases and a tested maximum replica count.Unbounded account-ID/email/merchant metric labels or full payload logging; avoid a monitoring stack that consumes most of a tiny VM.

The durable-commit/delivery distinction follows the transactional-outbox pattern. For PandaPay, preserve the existing business transaction and authorization boundaries when adding the worker; an external queue does not make a database write and message publish atomic by itself.

Practical edge deployment choice

A host-independent starting option is Cloudflare for edge delivery/security, with the existing API/auth origins behind it, exact public-cache rules, and private endpoints bypassed. An AWS-hosted alternative is CloudFront with the appropriate security/origin controls. Choose one initial edge platform based on supported features, region performance, quotas, cost and operational familiarity; neither is installed or selected by this review.

Use verified TLS to origin, private/firewalled upstreams and an origin-authentication strategy so attackers cannot simply bypass the edge. Trust client-IP headers only through the configured proxy chain, or all users may share one apparent IP—or callers may spoof it. Keep webhook signature checks. Avoid browser-only JavaScript challenges on native Flutter JSON endpoints unless the app has a supported integration. Origin restrictions, monitoring and proxy controls are separate deployment tasks (origin-protection guidance).

No CDN/WAF setting makes the app hacker-proof or repairs account-linking/RLS/session bugs. Edge TLS termination also introduces a processor of requests; keep secrets/financial payloads out of edge logs and review access/retention before routing them.

Acceptance tests and rollout order

  1. Establish no-store/bypass behavior first. Use two synthetic accounts and logged-out/invalid-token requests for the same private URL; verify bodies never cross accounts and shared-cache status is never a hit. Test query variants, encoded paths, misleading file suffixes, error statuses, Set-Cookie and every supported method. An Age header alone is not a complete cache-isolation test.
  2. Enable catalogue/categories caching in staging, verify a genuine cache hit and reduced origin requests, then publish/correct/withdraw a card. Check purge/version propagation, every supported app client's refresh path and the documented worst-case staleness. Test an edge miss and an unavailable origin.
  3. Exercise auth requests across two replicas, counter TTLs after partial failure, Redis outage/recovery and memory exhaustion. Confirm the intended shared limits and no unintended fail-open window.
  4. Test simultaneous cold-cache requests, mutation-versus-cache-population races, account switching and stale summary handling. Compare end-to-end p95 latency, DB query volume and origin bandwidth before/after; do not claim a fixed percentage saving in advance.
  5. Roll out one layer at a time with small traffic exposure and a rollback that bypasses the public cache without removing authentication. Keep campaign admission limits and DB connection budgets from section 13.

Priority for PandaPay: security fixes and cache privacy policy first; then CDN for public reads/assets plus shared Redis abuse controls before multi-instance auth; durable workers for heavy onboarding work; account-summary caches only if measurement justifies them. More infrastructure should remove a demonstrated bottleneck, not become another store of unbounded private data.

Skills used

  • Graphify: used the existing graph to locate related authentication/security/database code, expanding only from its vocabulary: auth, security, token, jwt, api, route, database, user, validation, refresh, otp, admin. The CDN/Redis follow-up used cache, catalogue, image, redis, static, version, queue, rate, limit for orientation. The graph is older than the checkout and that broad traversal was truncated, so findings were verified against current files and local metadata rather than accepted from the graph; provider behavior was checked in official documentation.
  • OWASP Mobile Security Checker, installed under /Users/chandresh_kerkar/.claude/skills/owasp-mobile-security-checker: used its four scanners and mobile checklist. Manual triage removed false HTTP/temporary-file alarms and kept outdated packages distinct from verified vulnerabilities. Backend review was explicitly outside that skill's scope and was performed separately.

Two server databases, distinct schemas

Database & schema boundaries

2 PostgreSQL databases · 3 database-scoped schema namespaces. The name public appears in both databases, but each is a separate namespace with its own tables. The pandapay schema inside the product database contains helper functions; it is distinct from the database with the same name.

DatabaseSchema namespaceTablesViewsApp functionsResponsibility
pandapaypandapay0030Product helper functions, including user context and access helpers
pandapaypublic8960Wallet, transactions, catalogue, rewards and application data
pandapay_authpublic701Identity, OTP, sessions, devices and authentication audit

Device storage: the app also uses SQLite for local financial stores, caches and queues. Its 19 source-defined tables are documented separately; SQLite is not a third backend database. System/internal PostgreSQL schemas are outside the application schema inventory.

pandapay.public.user_settings · Identity & wallet. 0 incoming foreign keys; 1 outgoing foreign keys.

Account-level client display/first-run preferences, synced across a user's devices (plan Phase 1.1). Opaque to the server: no api/ route, SQL function, or console screen reads individual keys. Per-device state stays in the client's own SharedPreferences and never lands here — notably the biometric app-lock flag, which is a property of one handset.

card_product_network_variants Source only

Verified alternative networks and network tiers for one card product; shares the parent product economics.

db/supabase/migrations/0043_card_product_network_variants.sql:9

create table card_product_network_variants (
  id                uuid primary key default gen_random_uuid(),
  card_product_id   uuid not null references card_products(id) on delete cascade,
  network           card_network not null,
  network_tier      text not null default 'N/A',
  label             text,
  source_url        text,

  is_active         boolean not null default true,

  constraint card_network_variant_must_be_known check (network::text <> 'unknown'),
  constraint card_network_variant_unique unique (card_product_id, network, network_tier)
);

  • All 19 active persistent SQLite table names were found in app/lib source. transaction_outbox_entries_new is a temporary migration replacement and is excluded.
  • The declarations contain no REFERENCES or FOREIGN KEY clauses. Identifiers such as user_card_id and transaction_id are logical links enforced by application/server behavior rather than SQLite foreign-key constraints.
  • Columns added by guarded runtime ALTER statements are shown separately from the initial CREATE TABLE declaration; column_count_after_runtime_updates includes them.
  • sync_state remains declared, while account_sync_state provides the account-scoped cursor. No DROP of sync_state was found in the inspected local schema sources.
  • local_needs_review is also created defensively in app/lib/data/needs_review_repository.dart:68; it is one table, not an additional table.
  • Financial cache, sync and import queues share account namespaces; this is a device cache/outbox design rather than a relational copy of every server table.

Views, enum types & application functions

pandapay

public.v_activation_funnel View
 SELECT date_trunc('week'::text, occurred_at)::date AS week,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE event = 'app_opened'::text) AS app_opened,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE event = 'onboarding_completed'::text) AS onboarding_completed,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE event = 'account_created'::text) AS account_created,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE event = 'first_card_added'::text) AS first_card_added,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE event = 'second_card_added'::text) AS second_card_added,
    count(*) FILTER (WHERE event = 'transaction_logged'::text) AS transaction_logged,
    count(DISTINCT profile_id) AS distinct_profiles
   FROM analytics_events
  GROUP BY (date_trunc('week'::text, occurred_at)::date)
  ORDER BY (date_trunc('week'::text, occurred_at)::date) DESC;
public.v_admin_card_catalogue_export View
 SELECT c.id,
    c.slug,
    c.name,
    c.network,
    c.card_type,
    c.status,
    c.data_version,
    c.verified_at,
    c.annual_fee_inr,
    c.joining_fee_inr,
    c.is_upi_linkable,
    c.art_asset,
    c.art_primary_color,
    c.point_value_inr,
    i.slug AS issuer_slug,
    i.name AS issuer_name,
    COALESCE(( SELECT jsonb_agg(to_jsonb(r.*) - 'card_product_id'::text) AS jsonb_agg
           FROM reward_rules r
          WHERE r.card_product_id = c.id), '[]'::jsonb) AS reward_rules,
    COALESCE(( SELECT jsonb_agg(to_jsonb(k.*) - 'card_product_id'::text) AS jsonb_agg
           FROM cap_rules k
          WHERE k.card_product_id = c.id), '[]'::jsonb) AS cap_rules,
    COALESCE(( SELECT jsonb_agg(to_jsonb(m.*) - 'card_product_id'::text) AS jsonb_agg
           FROM milestone_rules m
          WHERE m.card_product_id = c.id), '[]'::jsonb) AS milestone_rules,
    COALESCE(( SELECT jsonb_agg(to_jsonb(f.*) - 'card_product_id'::text) AS jsonb_agg
           FROM fee_waiver_rules f
          WHERE f.card_product_id = c.id), '[]'::jsonb) AS fee_waiver_rules,
    COALESCE(( SELECT jsonb_agg(to_jsonb(b.*) - 'card_product_id'::text) AS jsonb_agg
           FROM card_benefits b
          WHERE b.card_product_id = c.id), '[]'::jsonb) AS benefits,
    ( SELECT to_jsonb(x.*) - 'card_product_id'::text
           FROM forex_rules x
          WHERE x.card_product_id = c.id) AS forex,
    ( SELECT to_jsonb(y.*) - 'card_product_id'::text
           FROM fuel_surcharge_rules y
          WHERE y.card_product_id = c.id) AS fuel,
    ( SELECT to_jsonb(z.*) - 'card_product_id'::text
           FROM billing_cycle_rules z
          WHERE z.card_product_id = c.id) AS billing_cycle,
    COALESCE(( SELECT jsonb_agg(to_jsonb(rd.*) - 'card_product_id'::text) AS jsonb_agg
           FROM redemption_options rd
          WHERE rd.card_product_id = c.id), '[]'::jsonb) AS redemption_options,
    c.base_reward_unit,
    c.base_reward_rate,
    c.extended_data,
    c.excluded_categories,
    c.import_source_hash,
    c.import_source_run_id,
    c.imported_at,
    c.import_transform_version
   FROM card_products c
     JOIN issuers i ON i.id = c.issuer_id
  WHERE c.is_active;

           FROM cap_rules k
          WHERE k.card_product_id = c.id), '[]'::jsonb) AS cap_rules,

           FROM milestone_rules m
          WHERE m.card_product_id = c.id), '[]'::jsonb) AS milestone_rules,
    COALESCE(( SELECT jsonb_agg(to_jsonb(f.*) - 'card_product_id'::text) AS jsonb_agg
           FROM fee_waiver_rules f
          WHERE f.card_product_id = c.id), '[]'::jsonb) AS fee_waiver_rules,
    COALESCE(( SELECT jsonb_agg(to_jsonb(b.*) - 'card_product_id'::text) AS jsonb_agg
           FROM card_benefits b
          WHERE b.card_product_id = c.id), '[]'::jsonb) AS benefits,
    ( SELECT to_jsonb(x.*) - 'card_product_id'::text
           FROM forex_rules x

           FROM fuel_surcharge_rules y
          WHERE y.card_product_id = c.id) AS fuel,
    c.base_reward_unit,

  WHERE c.status = 'published'::publish_status AND c.is_active;
public.v_data_quality_dashboard View
 SELECT ( SELECT count(*) AS count
           FROM merchants) AS merchants_total,
    ( SELECT count(*) AS count
           FROM merchants
          WHERE merchants.is_published) AS merchants_published,
    ( SELECT count(*) AS count
           FROM merchants
          WHERE merchants.confidence = ANY (ARRAY['high'::record_confidence, 'operator_verified'::record_confidence])) AS merchants_high_conf,
    ( SELECT count(*) AS count
           FROM merchant_locations) AS locations_total,
    ( SELECT count(*) AS count
           FROM policy_change_alerts
          WHERE policy_change_alerts.state = 'open'::alert_state) AS alerts_open,
    ( SELECT count(*) AS count
           FROM data_error_reports
          WHERE data_error_reports.state = 'pending'::review_state) AS error_reports_pending,
    ( SELECT count(*) AS count
           FROM card_requests
          WHERE card_requests.state = 'pending'::review_state) AS card_requests_pending,
    ( SELECT count(*) AS count
           FROM merchant_conflicts
          WHERE merchant_conflicts.state = 'pending'::review_state) AS conflicts_pending,
    ( SELECT count(*) AS count
           FROM scrape_runs
          WHERE scrape_runs.status = 'failed'::scrape_status AND scrape_runs.started_at > (now() - '7 days'::interval)) AS scrape_failures_7d,
    ( SELECT count(*) AS count
           FROM card_products
          WHERE card_products.status = 'published'::publish_status) AS cards_published,
    ( SELECT count(*) AS count
           FROM card_products
          WHERE card_products.status = 'published'::publish_status AND card_products.verified_at < (now() - '180 days'::interval)) AS cards_stale_180d;
public.v_published_merchants View
 SELECT m.vpa,
    m.display_name,
    m.mcc,
    m.category_id,
    m.confidence,
    l.geohash6,
    l.grid_lat,
    l.grid_lng
   FROM merchants m
     LEFT JOIN merchant_locations l ON l.merchant_id = m.id
  WHERE m.is_published;
public.v_weekly_retention View
 WITH first_seen AS (
         SELECT analytics_events.profile_id,
            min(date_trunc('week'::text, analytics_events.occurred_at))::date AS cohort_week
           FROM analytics_events
          WHERE analytics_events.profile_id IS NOT NULL
          GROUP BY analytics_events.profile_id
        )
 SELECT f.cohort_week,
    date_trunc('week'::text, e.occurred_at)::date AS active_week,
    count(DISTINCT e.profile_id) AS active_profiles
   FROM analytics_events e
     JOIN first_seen f ON f.profile_id = e.profile_id
  WHERE e.profile_id IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY f.cohort_week, (date_trunc('week'::text, e.occurred_at)::date)
  ORDER BY f.cohort_week DESC, (date_trunc('week'::text, e.occurred_at)::date) DESC;
